You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
I woke before the alarm again, in that pale hour when the house has not quite decided to be a house and the street outside has not quite decided to be a street. The light was thin and grey and honest. It fell across the floorboards without warmth, found the edge of a book left open face down, found the cup from last night, found my shoes waiting by the door with the patience of animals. I lay there listening to the small sounds buildings make when they think nobody is awake, the tick of cooling pipes, the fridge humming its one low note, a distant door closing somewhere I would never identify, and I thought how strange it is that a life is mostly made of these intervals. Not the arrivals or the departures, not the ceremonies people photograph, but the kettle filling, the stairs taken slowly, the moment before the day asks anything of you.

I put the kettle on and stood at the window while it gathered itself toward boiling. Across the road a man was loading boxes into a van, bending and lifting with the practiced economy of someone who has done this in rain and dark and tiredness before. A woman walked past with a dog so small it seemed mostly made of determination. The dog stopped at every gate. The woman waited at every gate. Neither of them seemed impatient with the other, and I found myself absurdly moved by that, by the treaty they had clearly negotiated over years: we will go at the speed of curiosity. We will not hurry the world into being only useful. The kettle clicked off. I made tea too strong, as I always do when I am thinking about something else, and drank it anyway while the windows fogged a little at the corners.

I decided to walk to the sea, though walk is too purposeful a word for what I did. I drifted in that direction, taking the longer streets, the ones with cracked pavements and front gardens spilling over with rosemary and bicycles and bins and improbable gnomes faded to pastel. The town was waking in layers. First the bakers and the bus drivers, then the shopkeepers rolling up shutters with that metallic clatter that sounds like the day clearing its throat, then children being shepherded toward school with their bags bouncing and their negotiations already underway about gloves and homework and who had said what yesterday. Shop windows held their reflections. I saw myself pass through displays of shoes and fruit and wedding dresses, a ghost briefly assigned to commerce, here and gone. 

There is a hill at the edge of town where the houses give up and the gorse takes over, and from there you can see the water changing its mind about color. Some mornings it is slate. Some mornings it is hammered silver. Once, years ago, I saw it so calm and so blue that the horizon seemed less like a line than like an agreement the sky and sea had made to pretend to be separate. Today it was restless, crosshatched by wind, with white lines appearing and dissolving far out where the fishing boats moved like slow punctuation. I stood there with my hands in my pockets and did nothing important for a while. That used to make me uneasy, this standing. I was raised, as many of us were, on the suspicion that time must be justified. Now I suspect the opposite. The moments I remember most clearly are rarely the ones I filled efficiently. They are the bench, the shore, the kitchen threshold. The pause where the world got a chance to be noticed.

My grandfather had a shed that smelled of creosote and cold iron and the faint sweetness of cut wood. He was not a man who explained much. He mended things. He sharpened things. He kept screws in jam jars labeled in pencil with a hand so steady it looked printed until you got close and saw the humanity in it. When something broke in the house, a chair leg, a kettle handle, the catch on a gate, it would disappear into the shed and return days later not new, but more itself, bearing a small scar of wire or glue or a replacement part filed down to fit. I used to sit on an upturned bucket and watch his hands. He taught me, without ever announcing a lesson, that attention is a form of love that does not need to announce itself either. You look closely. You do not throw away too quickly. You learn the difference between ruined and merely tired.

I think about that shed whenever I pass the new blocks of flats going up by the old railway yard, all glass and render and brave names borrowed from trees that were cut down to build them. I am not nostalgic in the simple way people accuse each other of being nostalgic on the radio. I do not believe everything was better when the shops shut on Wednesdays and the buses were colder. I remember chilblains. I remember boredom so thick on Sunday afternoons it felt like weather. But I do miss a certain density of repair. The cobbler with his mouth full of tacks. The woman who could rewire a lamp while discussing the price of leeks. We have become brilliant at replacement and clumsy at maintenance, and perhaps that is true of more than objects. Friendships, marriages, neighborhoods, even our own bodies, we are encouraged to upgrade, to optimize, to move on, when sometimes what is wanted is a jam jar of screws and somebody willing to sit on an upturned bucket and look properly.

On the way down from the hill I took the path through the cemetery because it is quiet and because the shortcuts of the dead are often the most beautiful routes in a town. The stones lean at companionable angles. Some names have been softened by lichen into mere suggestions. Others are tended weekly, with flowers so fresh they startle. I read dates the way other people read headlines, doing the small arithmetic we all do, 1891 to 1917, 1946 to 1949, 1920 to 2009, that last one a whole library of a life, wars and rationing and television and grandchildren and the price of bread changing beyond recognition, all compressed into a dash. A blackbird was working the grass near a grave covered in ivy, utterly unconcerned with eternity. I liked him for it. Grief needs birds. It needs rain finding the collar of your coat and somebody putting the bins out beyond the wall, the ordinary continuing not as insult but as permission.

I came out by the library, which was just opening, and went in because libraries have never needed a reason beyond being there. The warmth hit me first, then that particular smell of paper and carpet and radiators and other people's coats. A toddler was conducting an intense negotiation with a cardboard box in the children's corner. An elderly man slept peacefully in the local history section with a newspaper tented over his face, rising and falling. At the desk, the librarian stamped a book with the old-fashioned thump that no software has improved upon, a sound like a small authoritative heart. I wandered the stacks without looking for anything, running a finger along spines, pulling out a volume of poems I did not know, a history of lighthouses, a field guide to clouds printed in 1973 with photographs that made every sky look heroic. This is one of the last places, I thought, where you are not required to be a customer. You may simply be a citizen of your own curiosity. You may sit. You may be warm. You may fail to produce anything at all and still be welcome among the atlases.

I found a table by the window and read about clouds for longer than intended. Cirrus, from the Latin for a lock of hair. Cumulus, a heap, a pile, the most generous of words for those summer towers that build themselves over fields all afternoon and promise rain they do not always deliver. I learned, or relearned, that a cloud is not an object but an event, a visible gathering of almost nothing, water changing its state in public. When I looked up, rain had started in earnest outside, needling the glass, darkening the pavement in patches like a map being drawn. People hurried. People did not hurry. A boy on a scooter went through a puddle with the pure scientific joy of discovering that consequences could be fun. I thought of all the vocabularies we have for things we love and how love often begins as naming. Once you know the word hogweed you see hogweed everywhere. Once someone teaches you to distinguish a swift from a swallow, the summer sky doubles its population. Language does not just describe the world. It issues invitations to notice it.

My mother wrote letters in a hand that slanted uphill as if every sentence were climbing toward better news. She wrote them at the kitchen table after supper, with the radio low, pausing sometimes to look out at the yard as though the next phrase might be found among the washing lines. She wrote to her sister, to old friends scattered by marriage and work, to me when I lived three streets away, because some things are easier to say without a face interrupting. I still have a bundle of them tied with the blue ribbon from a chocolate box, and I cannot read them in order. I dip. A recipe for soup becomes a paragraph about a neighbor's baby becomes a fierce opinion about a television programme neither of us could now identify. What strikes me is not the information. We have faster ways to move information. What strikes me is the time signature. A letter says: I sat with you in mind for twenty minutes. I chose this sentence over silence. In an age of instantaneous everything, the delay itself has become a kind of tenderness.

The rain eased by the time I left, leaving the town rinsed and reflective, every roof and bonnet holding a piece of sky. I bought bread and apples from the shop where the owner knows I will pretend to consider the expensive cheese and then not buy it, a ritual we both protect. On the counter there was a jar collecting for a football team, a handwritten sign about lost keys, a single glove pinned to a noticeboard like evidence in a very small crime. These noticeboards are the true newspapers of a place. Piano lessons. A kayak for sale. Someone offering to walk dogs, someone looking for a room, someone thanking whoever returned a cat named Biscuit. Civilization, I sometimes think, is not the monument in the square. It is the lost glove given a pin and a chance to be found.

In the afternoon I took a train two stops along the coast for no better reason than that I like trains and had nowhere I needed to justify. Trains permit a particular kind of thinking. You are moving but excused from steering. The landscape unspools without asking your opinion. A carriage is a temporary society with rules everyone understands: we will share this air, we will pretend not to listen, we will be strangely confessional if the journey is long enough. Across from me a young woman revised for an exam with highlighters in four colors and terror in her eyes. Beside her, a man in a suit ate a sandwich with the focused sadness of someone whose day had peaked early. Two teenagers shared one earphone each and laughed at something on a phone in that way that makes the whole world feel privately funny. When the conductor came through, he called everyone love or mate according to some internal weather system I could not decode but instantly trusted. We passed fields where horses stood in coats. We passed a caravan site, a sewage works, a field of solar panels tilting their dark faces to a sun currently behind cloud, all of it equal in the window, all of it briefly framed and therefore briefly beautiful.

I got off at a station consisting mostly of a shelter, a timetable, and a cat asleep on a bench as though employed to demonstrate relaxation. The village beyond had a pub, a post office clinging on inside a shop, and a beach where the tide had gone out so far it seemed to have forgotten something in another country. Wet sand held the light. Pools trapped whole skies. I walked out farther than was sensible in shoes not designed for theology, hopping between ribbed ridges of sand, past razor shells and the green glass of worn bottles and a crab shell emptied to the color of bone. Far away, tiny figures dug for something, lugworms or cockles or buried childhoods. The wind took the sound of them and gave nothing back. I felt the particular happiness that requires no witness and no improvement. My pockets slowly filled with shells I would later find and wonder at, having forgotten collecting them, as if a more hopeful version of me had left them there as evidence.

There is a photograph of me at about six on a beach like this, squinting, missing a front tooth, holding a bucket larger than my ambitions and wearing wellingtons on the wrong feet. I do not remember the day. I remember the photograph, which is a different thing, and perhaps that is how memory mostly works now. We remember the evidence. We build the day around it like scaffolding. Sometimes I worry the phone in my pocket has made a curator of me and robbed me of being a participant, archiving sunsets instead of watching them, but then I remember my grandmother describing a dance in 1943 in such detail, the band, the dress borrowed and altered, the boy who stepped on her foot and apologized so elaborately she married someone else entirely, that I could see the hall. She had no photograph of it. The telling was the technology. Maybe memory was never the event. Maybe it was always the story we could bear to keep retelling until it polished smooth in the hand, like those pieces of green glass in the sand, sharp once, safe now, still green when held to the light.

When I was twelve I wanted desperately to be interesting, which is the most exhausting ambition a person can have. I practiced signatures for a famous name I did not yet possess. I read the encyclopedia in the wrong order. I attempted to learn the trumpet, card tricks, and the names of constellations in the same month, and achieved a level of competence in each that could startle a stranger for approximately nine seconds. It took me years, decades if I am honest, to understand that interest is not a costume. It grows the way the garden behind the house grew, mostly when I was not supervising it. The plum tree my father planted and cursed for producing nothing fruited magnificently the summer after he stopped threatening to cut it down. Perhaps he just stopped noticing at the right season. Perhaps trees, like people, dislike being glared at by expectation. Now I am suspicious of grand plans for self improvement announced in January. I trust small repetitions done kindly. Read the page. Walk the hill. Write the letter badly rather than perfectly never. Put the screws in a jar and label it.

Speaking of gardens, I have become the kind of person who talks to tomato plants and pretends it is about carbon dioxide. This year I grew courgettes with the unstoppable enthusiasm they are famous for, giving them away to neighbors who began to cross the street to avoid another green torpedo in a carrier bag. I grew herbs I forgot to cook with and flowers I planted for bees whose names I am slowly learning. Solitary bees. Mason bees. Bees that look like tiny burglars and bees that look like flying embers. A garden teaches patience with a bluntness no book can manage. You cannot pull a carrot into growing faster. You cannot negotiate with a late frost. You can only prepare, and wait, and accept the slugs as the tax on tenderness. Some evenings I sit out there as the light fails and the blackbirds argue over the best roost, doing absolutely nothing in the vicinity of growing things, and it feels like the most honest work of the day.

I have been thinking lately about strangers, and how much of a life is held up by people whose names we will never know. The nurse who, years ago, held a basin and my dignity at the same time during a night in hospital I would rather forget and cannot. The bus driver who waited, actually waited, engine idling, while an old man with a stick made his slow way across wet tarmac, and then closed the doors as gently as if he were tucking the whole bus in. The woman in the supermarket queue who saw my card fail and my face do something I hope it did not do, and said, to the cashier and the air and me, "I think the machine did that to me this morning too," giving me thirty seconds to breathe. We call these small kindnesses, but scale is a liar. In the moment they are enormous. They are the difference between a day that confirms every suspicion you have about the world and a day that quietly files an objection.

At night the town changes its population. Foxes take the pavements. The takeaway signs buzz. From the hill road you can see windows lit in patterns that suggest a hundred separate novels all being lived simultaneously and none of them aware of the others, which is both lonely and, I find, deeply comforting. Someone is feeding a baby. Someone is revising, highlighting, terrified. Someone is dancing in a kitchen to a song from before they were born. Someone is sitting in the dark because the dark is, for now, simpler. The stars, when the cloud permits, arrange themselves with complete indifference to whether I can still find the Plough without thinking of my father's finger tracing it from a cold garden in winter, his breath clouding, saying there, and there, as if the sky were a map of somewhere we might one day be allowed to go. I never did learn all the constellations I promised that twelve-year-old I would. I know enough to feel accompanied.

I walked home under clearing skies with wet shoes and shells in my pockets and bread going slightly damp at the corner of the bag, and I passed the man with the van again, now empty, now locking up, nodding to me with the recognition of people who have shared a street at both ends of a day. The small dog had presumably inspected every gate to its satisfaction and gone in to dinner and dreams of gates. In my kitchen I put the shells on the windowsill in a line I would rearrange twice and then leave alone. I made soup from things that needed using, which is most good soups and, if I am honest, most good days. Onion, carrot, the end of a cabbage, a potato with opinions. While it simmered I read three pages of the lighthouse book and learned that the light at one rock station was once kept by a man who carved an entire chess set from driftwood during a single winter of storms and then, in spring, threw it piece by piece into the sea because, he said, the game was finished. I do not know if I believe him. I know I understand him. Some things we make only to prove to the storm that our hands remember what they are for.

Later I will sleep, and tomorrow the kettle will take its time, and the street will invent itself again, and perhaps I will walk a different way and notice a different glove on a different noticeboard, a different cat employed by a different station to teach the waiting world how to wait. Nothing will have been solved. The news will continue its fluent catastrophe. The inbox will refill like a tide that has read productivity books. And yet. The bread will still rise in the bakery on the corner. Somebody will still label a jar of screws in careful pencil. A blackbird will still work the grass among the gravestones, finding breakfast in eternity's garden, utterly unconcerned and completely correct. I will put on my shoes, which will be waiting with their animal patience by the door, and go out to meet the ordinary as if it were an appointment I had been looking forward to all my life, because on the good days, and increasingly on the others too, it is.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. The sample is a lyrical, first-person meditation that turns an ordinary day into a sustained reflection on attention, memory, repair, and kindness.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and gently elegiac, but not simply nostalgic: it remembers old shops, family rituals, and handwritten letters while acknowledging boredom, chilblains, and the limits of the past. Its pathos comes from treating small acts as meaningful without making them grand—the dog allowed to stop at every gate, a librarian’s stamp, a stranger giving someone time to recover from a failed card. Family memories of a grandfather who mended things and a mother who wrote letters give the reflections emotional weight. The reader is invited to slow down and notice ordinary life as a source of connection, not as a problem that must be optimized or solved.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample repeatedly foregrounds patient attention: to weather, birds, streets, books, gardens, and strangers. Repair recurs as both a literal practice and a moral image, from the grandfather’s shed and the jar of screws to relationships and neighborhoods. It also chooses to linger on mortality and memory—the cemetery, the grandmother’s story, the childhood photograph—without letting grief eclipse the ordinary continuance of life. Its central moral claim is that care often appears as time given, things maintained, and people noticed.

## Evidence line
> We have become brilliant at replacement and clumsy at maintenance, and perhaps that is true of more than objects.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the sample’s sustained attention to repair, everyday kindness, and deliberate noticing makes these choices unusually coherent and distinctive within the piece.

**Reflecting on maintenance vs. replacement**

I've been thinking about how we've gotten really good at replacing things but not so much at maintaining them. That feels true for more than just objects — it's almost a societal issue. It makes me curious about what this means for our values and lifestyles. Are we prioritizing the new and shiny over taking care of what we already have? It’s an interesting thing to consider!
